positions/restorationism/oneLine: The Church should restore the faith and practice of the New Testament church, setting aside later creeds, denominations and traditions, so that Christians can unite on the Bible alone.
positions/restorationism/coreClaims/0: The New Testament provides a pattern for church doctrine, worship and organisation.
positions/restorationism/coreClaims/1: Human creeds should not be tests of fellowship; "no creed but Christ, no book but the Bible".
positions/restorationism/coreClaims/2: Believers’ baptism by immersion "for the remission of sins" (Acts 2:38).
positions/restorationism/coreClaims/3: Weekly celebration of the Lord’s Supper.
positions/restorationism/coreClaims/4: Congregational autonomy with elders and deacons; use of Bible names for Bible things ("Christians", "churches of Christ").
positions/restorationism/origin: A broad primitivist impulse runs through Christian history (Waldensians, Anabaptists, Brethren), but the American Restoration Movement began with Barton W. Stone (after the Cane Ridge revival, 1801; the Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery, 1804) and Thomas and Alexander Campbell (Declaration and Address, 1809); their movements united in Lexington, Kentucky, in 1832. It divided into the Churches of Christ (a cappella, formally recognised 1906), the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ) and the independent Christian churches/churches of Christ. Many later movements (Adventists, Latter-day Saints, Pentecostals with their "apostolic faith") share restorationist premises.
positions/restorationism/strongestArgume: Scripture is the only universally accepted Christian authority, so it is the natural basis for unity.
Many historic divisions arise from post-biblical creeds and traditions.
It honours the Reformation principle of sola scriptura consistently.
Its emphasis on weekly communion and immersion reflects strong early-church evidence.
positions/restorationism/strongestObject: Historic churches argue that "no creed but the Bible" is itself a creed, and that the Bible must be interpreted within the community and its rule of faith, as the creeds do.
Ironically the movement itself split repeatedly (over instruments, missionary societies, theology).
Critics argue its teaching on baptism for remission of sins approaches baptismal regeneration and can foster legalism.
The New Testament may not provide a single, detailed blueprint for church order.
positions/restorationism/responses/0: Restorationists reply that their aim is not to deny historic Christianity but to subordinate all traditions to Scripture.
positions/restorationism/responses/1: Many now combine restorationist ideals with ecumenical engagement (the Disciples were founding members of the WCC).
positions/restorationism/consequences/0: Produced one of the largest American-born Christian movements, with millions of members in the US and growing churches in Africa, India and the Philippines.
positions/restorationism/consequences/1: Its primitivist logic, taken further, contributed to new religious movements claiming a fuller restoration.
positions/restorationism/consequences/2: The Disciples became a mainline ecumenical denomination; Churches of Christ remained conservative.
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/n: Latter-day Saint restoration (outside historic Nicene orthodoxy)
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/a: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
Mormonism (a name the church now asks to avoid)
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/o: Latter-day Saints believe that after a "Great Apostasy" God restored the original Church of Jesus Christ through the prophet Joseph Smith, with renewed priesthood authority, additional scripture and continuing revelation. Its teaching on God departs from the Nicene Creed, and Nicene churches do not regard it as within historic orthodoxy.
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/c: The early Church fell into apostasy, losing priesthood authority; God restored it through Joseph Smith (first vision 1820; church organised 6 April 1830).
The Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price are scripture alongside the Bible "as far as it is translated correctly".
The Godhead consists of three distinct divine beings united in purpose; the Father has a glorified body of flesh and bone (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22).
Humans existed premortally as spirit children of heavenly parents and can progress toward exaltation.
Saving ordinances (baptism, temple endowment, sealing) are performed by restored priesthood, including vicariously for the dead.
Living prophets and apostles continue to receive revelation.
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/k: Ezekiel 37:15–20 (read as Bible and Book of Mormon)
Book of Mormon; Doctrine and Covenants; Pearl of Great Price
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/o: Joseph Smith (1805–1844) emerged from the "burned-over district" of western New York amid revivals and restorationist ferment. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and led the church to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, Illinois, where he was killed in 1844. Brigham Young led the majority to Utah (1847); others formed the Reorganized Church (now Community of Christ, 1860). Plural marriage, publicly taught from 1852, was officially ended in 1890; the priesthood restriction on men of Black African descent was lifted in 1978.
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/s: Latter-day Saints argue that the proliferation of Christian denominations shows the need for restored divine authority and revelation (Joseph Smith’s question in James 1:5).
They point to the New Testament pattern of apostles, prophets and continuing revelation, which they believe historic churches lost.
They cite the lived fruit of the church: family life, service, missionary dedication and rapid growth to over 17 million members (2023).

Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches hold that its doctrine of God (multiple divine beings, an embodied Father, human exaltation) contradicts biblical monotheism and the Nicene Creed; the Catholic Church ruled LDS baptism invalid in 2001.
Historic Christians reject the claim of a total apostasy, citing Christ’s promise that the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church (Matt 16:18).

Historians and archaeologists find no independent evidence for the Book of Mormon’s ancient American civilisations, and critics raise questions about the Book of Abraham and early church history (polygamy, the 1857 Mountain Meadows massacre).
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/r: Latter-day Saints reply that they worship the Father, Son and Holy Ghost and accept Jesus Christ as divine Saviour, and that the Nicene formulations reflect later Greek philosophy.

The church has published essays (Gospel Topics, 2013–15) addressing historical controversies, and LDS scholars defend the Book of Mormon’s antiquity while affirming that its truth is known by spiritual witness (Moroni 10:4).
positions/latter-day-saint-restoration/c: Became the largest and most successful religious movement born in the United States, with a majority of members now outside the US.
Shaped the settlement and culture of Utah and the American West.
Its relationship to historic Christianity remains disputed: it calls itself Christian, while Nicene churches classify it as a distinct restorationist religion outside historic orthodoxy.
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/on: Jehovah’s Witnesses believe they have restored true Bible teaching: Jehovah alone is Almighty God, Jesus is his first created Son, Christ’s invisible kingdom rule began in 1914, and Armageddon will soon usher in an earthly paradise. Their rejection of the Trinity places them outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/co: Jehovah is the only true God; the Trinity is an unbiblical, post-apostolic doctrine.
Jesus is God’s firstborn creation, identified with Michael the archangel, who died on a stake as a ransom.
The holy spirit is God’s active force, not a person.
Christ began ruling invisibly in heaven in 1914; the present system will end soon at Armageddon.
144,000 anointed Christians will rule in heaven; a "great crowd" will live forever on a paradise earth; the wicked are annihilated, not tormented.
Members avoid blood transfusions, military service and political involvement, and witness door to door.
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/or: Charles Taze Russell (1852–1916), influenced by Adventist preachers in the post-1844 Millerite milieu, founded a Bible study group in Pittsburgh (c.1870) and Zion’s Watch Tower (1879). Under Joseph F. Rutherford the movement centralised and took the name Jehovah’s Witnesses (1931). The New World Translation appeared in 1950–61. Witnesses were persecuted in Nazi Germany (marked with a purple triangle in camps), and have been banned in the Soviet Union and in Russia since 2017.
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/st: Witnesses argue that strict monotheism is the plain teaching of both Testaments and that Trinitarian formulas are absent from Scripture.
They cite texts where Jesus calls the Father "greater" (John 14:28) or is called "firstborn of all creation" (Col 1:15).
Their commitment to neutrality and nonviolence (e.g. refusing to fight in Nazi Germany) and their evangelistic zeal are widely admired.
Nicene churches regard their Christology as a form of Arianism condemned at Nicaea (325), and cite texts calling Christ God (John 1:1; 20:28; Titus 2:13; Heb 1:8).
Scholars criticise the New World Translation’s renderings (e.g. "a god" in John 1:1) as theologically driven.
Failed or revised expectations (1914, 1925, 1975) and the redefinition of "this generation" are cited by critics and ex-members.

Practices such as shunning disfellowshipped members and refusing blood transfusions have drawn criticism, and child-abuse handling has been examined by courts and inquiries (e.g. Australian Royal Commission, 2015).
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/re: Witnesses reply that their translation follows the Greek grammar faithfully and restores the divine name.
They maintain that adjusting understanding as "the light gets brighter" (Prov 4:18) is part of faithful Bible study, not failed prophecy.
positions/jehovahs-witnesses-teaching/co: Grew to about 8.8 million active publishers in some 240 lands (2024 service year).
Their legal battles produced landmark religious-liberty rulings (e.g. US Supreme Court, West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943).
Remain separate from all other churches, which in turn classify them outside historic Christian orthodoxy.
positions/global-south-christianity/oneL: Christianity’s demographic and increasingly theological centre has moved to Africa, Latin America and Asia, where churches are typically Spirit-oriented, biblically and morally conservative, holistic and self-theologising.
positions/global-south-christianity/core: Christianity is a translatable faith that becomes at home in every culture (Walls, Sanneh).
Most Christians now live in the Global South, and their experience should shape theology, not only Western debates.
Many Southern churches emphasise the Holy Spirit, healing, deliverance and the reality of the spirit world.
Theology must address poverty, power, ancestors, other religions and nation-building in context.
Southern churches increasingly send missionaries to the West ("reverse mission").
positions/global-south-christianity/orig: The roots are ancient (Ethiopia, Egypt, India, the Church of the East), but the modern shift came through 19th- and 20th-century missions and especially indigenous movements: African prophets (William Wade Harris, 1913; Simon Kimbangu, 1921), African Instituted Churches, the Korean revivals (1907), Chinese indigenous churches (Watchman Nee, John Sung) and Latin American Pentecostalism (Chile, 1909; Brazil, 1911). After decolonisation, Christianity in Africa grew from about 10 million (1900) to several hundred million. Pew (2011) found that the share of Christians in Europe fell from about two-thirds in 1910 to about a quarter in 2010.
positions/global-south-christianity/stro: Demography: Africa now has more Christians than any other continent, and Latin America and Asia hold hundreds of millions more.
Indigenous leadership and vernacular Scripture have made Christianity an African, Asian and Latin American religion, not a Western import.
Southern churches often embody New Testament vitality: growth, evangelism, healing, community under persecution.
Critics warn of prosperity theology, authoritarian "big man" leadership and syncretism in some fast-growing churches.
Western progressive critics object to Southern churches’ conservative sexual ethics (e.g. in the Anglican Communion conflict).
Some scholars caution against generalising about a vast, diverse "Global South" or ignoring its long Orthodox and Catholic histories.
positions/global-south-christianity/resp: Southern theologians reply that discernment of syncretism applies equally to Western accommodation to secular culture.
They insist that Southern Christians must be heard as theologians in their own right, not merely as objects of Western concern.
positions/global-south-christianity/cons: Reshaped world Christian demography, mission and leadership (e.g. the first Latin American pope, 2013).
Realigned Anglican and Methodist communions (GAFCON 2008; Global Methodist Church 2022).
Brought new questions (ancestors, polygamy, spiritual warfare, poverty) to the centre of theology.
